The house of David will look on the one they have pierced and mourn, family by family, as for an only child.
Jesus joins the two texts: the tribes mourn and see the Son of Man coming on the clouds with power and great glory.
Before the high priest Jesus claims Daniel 7:13 and Psalm 110:1 for himself, which the council hears as blasphemy.
John cites Zechariah 12:10 at the piercing of Jesus' side, so the pierced one is identified with the crucified Jesus.
He is coming with the clouds and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all the tribes will wail.
One like a son of man walks among the lampstands, with white hair drawn from Daniel's Ancient of Days.
One like a son of man seated on a white cloud, wearing a golden crown and holding a sickle, begins the harvest of the earth.

In Daniel a human figure, contrasted with the beasts from the sea, is brought to God and given the kingdom, and the vision is linked to the holy ones who receive the kingdom. Jesus used the title for himself and combined it with Zechariah's pierced one, so that vindication and mourning belong together. Revelation draws the threads into one figure: the crucified and risen Jesus who shares God's throne and comes in judgment and rule.

In Canaanite texts from Ugarit, Baal is called the rider of the clouds, and in the Hebrew Bible clouds are the vehicle of the LORD himself (Psalm 104:3, Isaiah 19:1), so a human figure riding them was striking. Second Temple writings developed Daniel's figure: the Similitudes of 1 Enoch (chapters 37 to 71) describe a pre-existent Son of Man, the Chosen One, who sits on the throne of glory and judges kings, and 4 Ezra 13 has a man rising from the sea and flying with the clouds. In the Greco-Roman world a ruler's arrival was celebrated as a parousia, but Revelation's arriving king is one who was pierced.

Revelation 1:7 fuses Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 12:10 exactly as Matthew 24:30 does, and widens Zechariah's mourning clans of Israel to all the tribes of the earth (or of the land). In 1:13-14 the son of man is given the white hair of the Ancient of Days, merging the two figures of Daniel 7 in a way Daniel does not. Daniel's figure goes up to God; in Revelation 1:7 the direction is usually taken as coming to earth, though some read Daniel's sense of enthronement into it.

Preterists commonly read Revelation 1:7 as Christ's coming in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, with the tribes of the land as Israel, while futurists and most historicists see the visible bodily second coming at the end of the age. Idealists stress the enthroned Christ present to his churches now, whose final coming the text also anticipates.
The Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last
Isaiah's claim that the LORD alone is first and last is spoken by God and then by Jesus in Revelation's opening and closing.
The LORD who called the generations from the beginning says: I, the LORD, the first, and with the last, I am he.
I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god, a challenge to the idols to predict the future.
Listen to me, O Jacob: I am he, I am the first, and I am the last, the creator who also redeems from Babylon.
The Lord God, who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty, says: I am the Alpha and the Omega.
The risen Jesus says: I am the first and the last, and the living one; I died, and behold I am alive for evermore.
To suffering Smyrna, the speaker is the first and the last, who died and came to life.
From the throne God says: It is done, I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end.
Jesus combines all three forms: the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.

In Isaiah the phrase asserts that the God of Israel alone stands at the start and the end of history, which is why he alone can announce what is coming and save his people from Babylon. Revelation uses it to frame the whole book: history begins and ends with God. Because Jesus speaks the same words that God speaks in 1:8 and 21:6, the title becomes one of the book's clearest ways of including Jesus within the identity of the one God.

Alpha and omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, a merism meaning everything from beginning to end. Later rabbinic tradition made a similar point with Hebrew letters, saying the seal of God is emet, truth, spelled with the first, middle and last letters of the alphabet (Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 55a). Greek religious language also spoke of a god as beginning, middle and end (an Orphic line about Zeus, and Josephus, Against Apion 2.190, uses it of Israel's God), so Asian readers would hear a claim to total sovereignty that rivals pagan and imperial claims.

Isaiah's first and last is a polemic against idols; Revelation turns it against the beast and Babylon, whose power is temporary. The striking development is the transfer: the title God uses of himself in Isaiah and in Revelation 1:8 and 21:6 is used by Jesus in 1:17, 2:8 and 22:13. Revelation also expands the single phrase into a triple form at its close.

The schools differ little here, since all read the title as a statement about the sovereignty of God and the divine status of Christ. Differences concern only how that sovereignty works out in the events of the book, whether in the first century, across church history, at the end, or in every age.
Who is and who was and who is to come
An expansion of the divine name revealed to Moses, reshaped so that God's future is not merely that he will be, but that he is coming.
God tells Moses: I am who I am (ehyeh asher ehyeh); the Greek translation renders it I am the one who is (ho on).
See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god beside me; a verse the Targums expand with past, present and future.
I, the LORD, the first, and with the last, I am he: the divine name spanning all generations.
Grace and peace from him who is and who was and who is to come, kept unchanged in Greek even after the preposition from.
The Lord God, the Almighty, names himself with the same threefold formula alongside the Alpha and the Omega.
The four living creatures sing it day and night, in the order who was and is and is to come.
At the seventh trumpet the elders thank the one who is and who was, without who is to come, because he has begun to reign.
The angel of the waters praises the one who is and who was, the Holy One, for his just judgments.

The formula expands the divine name of Exodus 3:14 into an affirmation that God is the living God in every tense. Its third member is not who will be but who is coming, so God's future is pictured as his arrival to set the world right. When that coming is celebrated in 11:17 and 16:5, the third member drops out, which suggests the book is tracking the arrival of what it promised.

The Greek Old Testament rendered Exodus 3:14 as ego eimi ho on, I am the one who is, and Jewish Aramaic Targums expanded the name; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Deuteronomy 32:39 has God say that he is the one who is and who was and who will be. Greek religion had similar threefold formulas: Pausanias records a song of the priestesses at Dodona, Zeus was, Zeus is, Zeus will be. Hearers in Asia would recognise the form, but Revelation's version ends with coming, not simply continuing.

Revelation follows the Jewish expansion of the name but changes the future tense to a present participle, the coming one, tying the name to the theme of God's and Christ's coming. In 1:4 it treats the whole phrase as an indeclinable name, breaking ordinary Greek grammar, probably on purpose to preserve the name's form as Exodus 3:14 does. In 11:17 and 16:5 the dropping of the third member reverses the earlier pattern and marks the coming as having arrived.

All the schools read the formula as a statement of God's eternity and sovereignty. They differ on what the arrival marked in 11:17 and 16:5 refers to: preterists often link it to judgment in the first century, historicists to later historical turning points, futurists to the end-time kingdom, and idealists to the final consummation that every judgment anticipates.
Holy, holy, holy
The seraphim's threefold cry in Isaiah's temple vision, sung in the synagogue, becomes the unceasing song of heaven's throne room.
A kingship psalm repeats three times that the LORD enthroned above the cherubim is holy.
Isaiah sees the Lord on a high throne, and six-winged seraphim call: Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.
Four living creatures, each with faces of a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle, bear the throne-chariot of God.
A great voice blesses the glory of the LORD from its place, a verse later paired with Isaiah 6:3 in synagogue prayer.
John says Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus' glory, linking the temple vision to Christ.
Four living creatures full of eyes, each with six wings, never cease to say: Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come.
The victors by the sea sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb: who will not fear, O Lord, for you alone are holy.

The threefold repetition is a Hebrew way of giving the strongest possible emphasis: God's holiness is absolute and his glory fills creation. In Isaiah the vision leads to confession, cleansing and commissioning, and in Revelation it is the centre from which all the judgments and the redemption of the book flow. The song shows that heaven's worship is the true reality behind the earthly struggles that follow.

In synagogue liturgy the Kedushah, recited within the Amidah, joins Isaiah 6:3 with Ezekiel 3:12, so that the congregation joins the angels' praise; its exact date of origin is debated, but angelic praise of this kind is already found in Second Temple texts such as 1 Enoch 39:12 (Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of spirits) and the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice at Qumran. Early Christians used the Sanctus too (1 Clement 34:6 cites Isaiah 6:3). In Roman Asia, choirs of hymn singers (hymnodes) praised the emperor in the imperial cult, so heavenly hymns to God and the Lamb set up a pointed contrast.

Revelation combines Isaiah's six-winged seraphim with Ezekiel's four living creatures, simplifying Ezekiel's four faces into one face per creature and moving their eyes onto the creatures themselves. It replaces Isaiah's the whole earth is full of his glory with who was and is and is to come, since in the story of Revelation the earth is not yet visibly filled with his glory and his coming is still the goal. The scene in chapter 4 is then extended in chapter 5 so that the Lamb receives the same worship.

There is broad agreement that chapter 4 depicts the heavenly throne room. Some dispensational futurists read the summons of 4:1 as a picture of the church's rapture before the tribulation, while other futurists, preterists, historicists and idealists read it as John's visionary access to heaven, a scene of worship that holds true throughout history.
The bride and the marriage supper of the Lamb
The prophets' picture of God as Israel's husband ends in Revelation with the Lamb's wedding and a bride-city adorned for him.
My sister, my bride: the poem celebrates love between a bridegroom and bride, read by later Jews and Christians as a picture of God and his people.
Your Maker is your husband: forsaken Zion is called back like a wife deserted in youth; compare 62:5, as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride.
He has clothed me with garments of salvation, as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.
The LORD enters a covenant with Jerusalem, spreads his garment over her, washes her and clothes her in fine linen and jewels.
After unfaithfulness, God promises to betroth Israel to himself for ever in righteousness, steadfast love and faithfulness.
John the Baptist calls Jesus the bridegroom who has the bride, and himself the friend who rejoices at his voice; compare the wedding parables of Matthew 22 and 25.
Christ loved the church and gave himself for her, to cleanse her and present her to himself in splendour, without spot.
The marriage of the Lamb has come and his bride has made herself ready, granted fine linen, which is the righteous deeds of the saints; blessed are those invited to the supper.
The new Jerusalem comes down from God prepared as a bride adorned for her husband; in 21:9 the bride is shown as the holy city.

Across the canon marriage is a picture of covenant: God binds himself to his people in faithful love, and their idolatry is described as adultery. The prophets look beyond betrayal to a renewed betrothal, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the bridegroom and the church as his bride. Revelation brings the image to its wedding day, when the bride's preparation is complete and God dwells with his people (Revelation 22:17 adds that the Spirit and the bride say, Come).

A Jewish marriage began with a legally binding betrothal, often with a bride price, followed by an interval in which the bride prepared and was adorned; then the groom came, often at night with lamps and friends, to bring her in procession to his home, where a wedding feast could last up to seven days (Judges 14:12, Tobit 11:18, Matthew 25:1-13). Greco-Roman weddings likewise centred on the evening procession of the bride to the groom's house. Revelation's readers would hear the cry the marriage has come and the bride has made herself ready as the climax of that familiar sequence.

Revelation intensifies the prophets' hope by moving from restored marriage to the wedding itself, and it pairs the bride with her opposite, the harlot Babylon: both are women and cities, both are dressed in fine linen, and both are introduced by an angel's come, I will show you (17:1, 21:9). The bride's linen is granted to her yet described as the saints' righteous deeds, balancing gift and faithfulness. Unlike Ezekiel 16 and Hosea, there is no further fall: the bride is presented spotless, as Ephesians 5 anticipated.

Preterists often see the new covenant people as the bride replacing a faithless Jerusalem after AD 70, historicists and futurists place the marriage supper at the culmination of history after Christ's return, with some dispensationalists distinguishing the church as bride from Israel and the guests, and idealists see the union of Christ and his people as begun now and perfected at the end.
The harlot
The prophets used prostitution for Jerusalem's idolatry and for the trade and seduction of Tyre, Nineveh and Babylon; Revelation draws them into one great harlot.
How the faithful city has become a whore, she who was full of justice: Jerusalem itself is the first harlot city.
Tyre is sung of as a forgotten prostitute who will return to her hire and prostitute herself with all the kingdoms of the world.
Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand that made the nations drunk, a city dwelling by many waters.
Jerusalem trusts in her beauty and plays the whore with every passer-by; Ezekiel 23 retells it as the two sisters Oholah and Oholibah.
Israel, the mother, has played the whore, chasing lovers who give her bread, wool, flax and oil.
Nineveh falls for the countless whorings of the prostitute, graceful and of deadly charms, mistress of sorceries who sells nations.
The great prostitute seated on many waters and on a scarlet beast, dressed in purple and scarlet, holds a golden cup and is drunk with the blood of the saints.
The nations have drunk the wine of her passion, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from her luxury.
Heaven rejoices that God has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth and avenged the blood of his servants.

In the prophets harlotry has two faces: covenant unfaithfulness by God's own people, and the seductive power of wealthy, idolatrous cities that sell themselves and others for gain. Revelation's Babylon combines both: she seduces the nations into idolatry and luxury, trades in human lives (18:13), and persecutes the saints. Her judgment is the necessary counterpart to the bride's wedding.

In the Ancient Near East, covenant was often pictured as marriage, so idolatry was naturally described as adultery and alliances with foreign powers as prostitution; trade cities like Tyre were also said to earn a harlot's hire. In the Roman province of Asia the goddess Roma, the city of Rome personified, was worshipped with temples (Smyrna built one in 195 BC, and Pergamum honoured Roma and Augustus together), and a sestertius of Vespasian (AD 71) shows Roma seated on seven hills by the Tiber. Some commentators also note Roman references to prostitutes displaying their names, which may lie behind the name on the harlot's forehead (17:5).

Revelation gathers Jeremiah's Babylon (golden cup, many waters), Isaiah's Tyre (trade with the kings of the earth, closely followed in the laments of chapter 18 and Ezekiel 27) and Nahum's Nineveh (sorceries) into a single figure. It intensifies the picture: she is not only unfaithful but drunk with the blood of the saints. Unlike Hosea and Ezekiel 16, where the harlot wife is finally restored, Revelation's harlot is destroyed, and the role of restored wife belongs to the bride instead.

Many preterists and idealists see Babylon as Rome or the Roman order, while some preterists identify her as apostate Jerusalem because of the prophets' harlot language and 11:8; classic Protestant historicists saw papal Rome, futurists expect an end-time religious, economic or literal rebuilt city, and idealists see the seductive world system present in every age.
The harvest and the winepress
Joel's sickle and Isaiah's blood-red winepress become Revelation's twin harvests of the earth and the Rider's treading of God's wrath.
A warrior comes from Edom in crimson garments: I have trodden the winepress alone, and their lifeblood spattered my garments.
The Lord has trodden as in a winepress the virgin daughter of Judah, so even Jerusalem can be the vintage.
Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe; go in, tread, for the winepress is full, in the valley of decision (3:14).
In the parable of the weeds the harvest is the end of the age and the reapers are angels.
One like a son of man on a cloud swings his sickle and the earth is reaped, for its harvest is fully ripe.
An angel gathers the vine of the earth into the great winepress of the wrath of God, and blood flows to the horses' bridles for 1,600 stadia.
The Rider wears a robe dipped in blood and treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty.

Harvest pictures the end of a season when everything is gathered and sorted, and the winepress pictures crushing judgment, red juice standing for blood. Across the canon both images express God's final reckoning with evil, though harvest can also mean gathering people in (Matthew 9:37-38, John 4:35). Revelation uses both to show that history ripens toward a decisive judgment carried out by God and his Messiah.

In the Levant grapes were trodden by foot in rock-cut vats, and the treaders' clothes were stained red, which makes Isaiah 63's image vivid; grain harvest and vintage were the two great agricultural climaxes of the year, with festivals to match. Second Temple apocalyptic used similar pictures of overwhelming slaughter: 1 Enoch 100:3 says a horse will walk up to its breast in the blood of sinners. Readers in Asia, where vineyards were common, would recognise the scene immediately.

Revelation 14 splits Joel 3:13's two lines into two scenes, a grain harvest and a vintage, and puts the son of man of Daniel 7 in charge of the first. Isaiah 63's warrior has blood on his garments after treading; in Revelation 19:13 the Rider's robe is already dipped in blood before the battle, which some take as his own blood or the martyrs' and others as anticipating the enemies' blood. The 1,600 stadia (about 300 km) is a vast intensification of the prophetic image.

Interpreters debate whether the grain harvest of 14:14-16 is the gathering of the saved or, with the vintage, a scene of judgment. Preterists often tie the 1,600 stadia to the length of the land of Israel and judgment in the Jewish War, historicists to particular historical judgments, futurists to Armageddon at Christ's return, and idealists to the final judgment portrayed symbolically.
The Day of the LORD and the great day of wrath
The prophets' dreaded day when God intervenes to judge and save becomes in Revelation the great day of the wrath of God and the Lamb.
The day of the LORD comes, cruel with wrath, and the stars, sun and moon give no light, an oracle against Babylon.
The sun turns to darkness and the moon to blood before the great and awesome day of the LORD, later quoted by Peter in Acts 2:20.
Woe to you who desire the day of the LORD: it is darkness, not light, for Israel itself.
The great day of the LORD is near, a day of wrath, distress, ruin and darkness.
God will send Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes.
The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night, unexpectedly for those who say peace and security.
The day of the Lord will come like a thief, and the heavens will pass away and the earth be exposed.
At the sixth seal sun darkens, moon becomes like blood, and people cry that the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?
Demonic spirits gather the kings for battle on the great day of God the Almighty, with the warning: I am coming like a thief.

The Day of the LORD is the time when God personally acts to put down his enemies, purge his people and establish his rule. The prophets apply it to near events, such as Babylon's fall or a locust plague, and to a final day, and Amos warns that it brings judgment on complacent Israel too. The New Testament makes it the day of the Lord Jesus, coming unexpectedly like a thief, and Revelation portrays it as the great day of the wrath of God and the Lamb.

Scholars connect the Day of the LORD to Ancient Near Eastern traditions of the divine warrior who goes out to battle, with cosmic upheaval as the language of theophany, and Amos shows that the hope was already popular in eighth century Israel. Second Temple texts such as 1 Enoch speak often of the great day of judgment. The thief image fits a world without street lighting or police, where security depended on watchfulness.

Revelation 6:12-17 gathers the cosmic signs of Joel 2:31 and Isaiah 34:4, the hiding in rocks of Isaiah 2:19 and the cry to the mountains of Hosea 10:8, and Malachi 3:2's who can endure the day. Its decisive change is that the wrath is the wrath of the Lamb as well as of God. Revelation 16:15 repeats Jesus' thief saying (Matthew 24:43, compare 3:3), so the Day remains both dreaded and unexpected.

Preterists often apply the sixth seal to the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, classic historicists to the fall of pagan Rome in the time of Constantine, futurists to the end-time tribulation (with pretribulational and prewrath writers disagreeing on when the day of wrath begins), and idealists to a picture of final judgment that recurring judgments foreshadow.
Come out of her, my people
The prophets' summons to flee Babylon and go home becomes Revelation's urgent call to separate from the doomed city.
The angels urge Lot to bring his family out of Sodom, lest they be swept away in the punishment of the city.
Go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea; proclaim to the end of the earth that the LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob.
Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing, you who bear the vessels of the LORD.
Flee from the midst of Babylon and go out of the land of the Chaldeans, like male goats before the flock.
Flee from the midst of Babylon; let every one save his life; be not cut off in her punishment.
Go out of the midst of her, my people! Let every one save his life from the fierce anger of the LORD.
Paul applies Isaiah 52:11 to the church: go out from their midst and be separate, and touch no unclean thing.
Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins and share her plagues, for her sins are heaped high as heaven.

In Isaiah and Jeremiah the call is to leave a doomed empire and return to Zion, a new exodus made possible by God's judgment on Babylon. Paul turns it into a call for the church to keep itself from idolatry, and Revelation addresses it to believers who are tempted to share in Babylon's sins and profits. The phrase combines warning, rescue and identity: God's people do not belong to the city that is about to fall.

For the Judean exiles, Babylon's fall to Cyrus in 539 BC made literal departure possible, and the prophets framed it as a second exodus. In Roman Asia, believers were drawn into imperial cult festivals, trade guild banquets with food offered to idols, and a Mediterranean economy centred on Rome (Revelation 2:14, 2:20, 18:11-19), so coming out could mean costly economic and social withdrawal. Eusebius later reports that the Jerusalem church fled to Pella before the city's fall, an episode some readers connect with this call.

Revelation 18:4 reproduces Jeremiah 51:45 almost word for word and echoes Jeremiah 51:6 and 51:9 (her judgment reaches to heaven). What was a geographic journey home in the prophets becomes, for most readers, a call to moral and religious separation, as in 2 Corinthians 6:17, though some see a literal flight. The added reason, lest you take part in her sins, intensifies the call from escaping punishment to avoiding complicity.

Preterists who identify Babylon with Jerusalem link the call to Christians leaving the city before AD 70, while those who see Rome read it as separation from Roman idolatry and commerce. Historicists of the Reformation era applied it to leaving the Roman church, futurists to believers in an end-time Babylon, and idealists to a standing call to every generation to refuse compromise.
I am coming soon; Come, Lord Jesus (Maranatha)
Isaiah's promise that the LORD comes with his reward becomes Jesus' repeated I am coming soon, answered by the church's ancient prayer, Come, Lord Jesus.
Behold, the Lord GOD comes with might; behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him.
Say to the daughter of Zion: behold, your salvation comes; behold, his reward is with him.
The vision awaits its appointed time; if it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come, it will not delay (applied in Hebrews 10:37 to the coming one).
The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; but who can endure the day of his coming?
Paul closes a Greek letter with the Aramaic prayer Maranatha, Our Lord, come.
Behold, I am coming soon; blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.
Behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done.
He who testifies says, Surely I am coming soon; and the book answers, Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!

The thread runs from God's promise to come and set things right to the church's prayer for Jesus to come. Revelation repeats I am coming (compare 2:16, 3:11, 16:15) to give its readers hope and urgency, and it ends not with a description but with a prayer. The emphasis is on readiness: keeping the words of the book, holding fast and longing for his arrival.

Maranatha is Aramaic and can be divided as marana tha, Our Lord, come, or maran atha, Our Lord has come; the prayer of Revelation 22:20 favours the first, and the Didache (10:6) uses Maranatha in its eucharistic prayers, showing it was early Christian worship language carried over untranslated. In the Greco-Roman world a ruler's parousia or adventus was a public event for which a city prepared with festivals, processions and honours, and coins celebrated imperial arrivals. Christians borrowed the vocabulary for the arrival of their Lord.

Revelation 22:12 echoes Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11 almost exactly, but the one who comes with his recompense is now Jesus, not the LORD of Isaiah. The prophets' he comes becomes the first person I am coming, and the community's answer turns Paul's Aramaic Maranatha into Greek, Come, Lord Jesus. Habakkuk's it will not delay supplies the note of certainty behind soon.

Preterists take soon in its plain sense of a coming in judgment within the first readers' lifetime, fulfilled in the events of AD 66 to 70 (most still also expect a future final coming), while futurists read it as sudden or as near from God's perspective (2 Peter 3:8). Historicists see the promise worked out across a long series of events, and idealists see the imminence as a constant posture of readiness for every generation.
King of kings and Lord of lords: the rider on the white horse
A divine title and an imperial boast meet in the Rider of Revelation 19, who conquers with the sword of his mouth.
The LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, mighty and awesome God who is not partial.
The LORD's anointed king will break the rebel nations with a rod of iron (Greek: shepherd them with a rod of iron).
The shoot of Jesse will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth and slay the wicked with the breath of his lips.
The Servant says: he made my mouth like a sharp sword.
Daniel addresses Nebuchadnezzar as king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given the kingdom; compare Ezekiel 26:7 and Ezra 7:12.
God is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who will display Christ's appearing at the proper time.
From the mouth of the one like a son of man comes a sharp two-edged sword.
The kings with the beast make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb conquers them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings.
The Rider called Faithful and True, the Word of God, strikes the nations with the sword from his mouth, and on his robe and thigh is written King of kings and Lord of lords.

The title asserts supreme sovereignty: God, and in Revelation the Lamb, rules over every ruler. The Old Testament applies it to God, while human emperors such as Nebuchadnezzar held a version only as a gift from God. Revelation gives the title to the Lamb who conquers by his death and by his word, and it pictures his final victory as a Rider whose only weapon is the sword of his mouth.

King of kings was a royal title of Assyrian and especially Persian kings (used by Darius in the Behistun inscription and by Artaxerxes in Ezra 7:12), and Second Temple Jews applied it to God (2 Maccabees 13:4, 1 Enoch 9:4). Suetonius reports that Domitian liked to be called dominus et deus noster, our lord and god, and Roman generals celebrated victories with a triumph, riding a chariot drawn by white horses through the city. Revelation's Rider, followed by white-clad armies, would read as a rival triumph that exposes imperial claims.
